issues.source_quote: Это тебе не мелочь по карманам тырить!
issues.justification: The Russian means 'This isn't petty pickpocketing / stealing loose change from pockets.' The criminal slang and taunting contrast are weakened; 'pocketing loose change' sounds flat and idiomatic in the wrong way, losing the underworld voice.

issues.source_quote: Все! Кина не будет. Электричество кончилось.
issues.translation_quote: That's it. No movie. The electricity's run out.
issues.justification: This is a famous comic line with deliberately uneducated, deadpan phrasing. 'No movie' is too literal and doesn't recreate the bumbling comic register; a colloquial line like 'Show's over—power's out' would better preserve the joke.

issues.translation_quote: gouge his peepers out / I'll gouge your peepers out
issues.justification: While slangy, 'peepers' is tonally off: it sounds playful/cartoonish rather than menacing Soviet-criminal argot. This recurring catchphrase is central to the character voice, and the chosen equivalent weakens both menace and comic edge.

issues.translation_quote: You've made it a daisy-chain: Remember-don't remember.
issues.justification: This literalizes an idiomatic comic phrase into nonsense. «Ромашка» alludes to the childish game 'loves me, loves me not,' i.e. repetitive back-and-forth. 'Daisy-chain' does not land as humor and sounds wrong in English.

This refers back to the repeated cry to the camel-handler and means 'same as the camel [you were addressing].' 'Like the camel' is opaque in English and loses the callback joke unless rephrased more helpfully.

issues.source_quote: этот... нехороший человек... мне на ногу батарею сбросил, падла!
issues.translation_quote: this... bad person... dropped a radiator on my foot, the bastard!
issues.justification: The joke is that, under orders to speak 'civilian language,' he begins politely and then involuntarily reverts to criminal abuse. 'The bastard' softens and generalizes «падла»; the comic register-switch is blunted.
A literal calque of criminal slang. In English 'stitch him up' usually means frame him, not kill him, so even if context saves it, the phrase is awkward and misleading.
Not wrong, but 'Go ahead' would be more natural here when asking to look at a photo/document.
